findings.regulator: US Department of Justice (DOJ); overwhelmingly enforced via private ADA lawsuits

obligations: Provide a website accessible to people with disabilities; courts and DOJ measure conformance against WCAG (2.0/2.1 Level AA)
Offer an accessible alternative contact route where full conformance is not yet achieved
frameworks.why: Website accessibility suits and demand letters number in the thousands each year; they target obvious WCAG failures (missing alt text, unlabeled forms, poor contrast) that a scan surfaces immediately.
frameworks.focus: Can a screen-reader and keyboard-only user complete the same core tasks (browse, add to cart, check out, contact you) as everyone else?

frameworks.name: CAN-SPAM Act — commercial email requirements
frameworks.regulator: Federal Trade Commission (FTC); also enforceable by state AGs and ISPs
frameworks.citation: Controlling the Assault of Non-Solicited Pornography And Marketing Act of 2003, 15 U.S.C. §§7701-7713; FTC CAN-SPAM Rule, 16 CFR Part 316

penalty.basis: civil penalties up to $53,088 per non-compliant email (2025 adjustment); aggregate judgments reach the millions where volume is high

obligations: Every commercial email must carry accurate routing and a valid physical postal address
Provide a clear opt-out and honour it (opt-out model, not opt-in)
frameworks.why: CAN-SPAM is a per-email liability; a newsletter footer missing a postal address or a broken unsubscribe multiplies fast across a send list.
frameworks.focus: Does every marketing email carry a real postal address and a one-click unsubscribe you honour within ten business days?

frameworks.name: FTC Act Section 5 - Unfair or Deceptive Practices (Health Data and Privacy Claims)

penalty.basis: FTC Act Section 5 carries no general civil penalty for a first unfair/deceptive act; relief is consumer redress, disgorgement and injunctive bans. A civil penalty (up to 53,088 dollars per violation, 16 CFR 1.98, 15 U.S.C. 45(l)/(m)) attaches only where the conduct violates a prior FTC order or a specific FTC rule

obligations: Ensure privacy and security representations are truthful and not contradicted by actual data flows
frameworks.why: The BetterHelp and Cerebral cases turned ordinary marketing pixels plus a privacy promise into multi-million-dollar orders; the deceptive gap is between the stated policy and the actual data flows.
frameworks.focus: Do the site privacy claims (including any 'HIPAA compliant' badge) match where consumer data actually goes?

enforcement.summary: 7.8m consumer refund and a ban on sharing health data for advertising, after disclosing email, IP and mental-health questionnaire data to Facebook, Snapchat, Criteo and Pinterest despite privacy promises.

frameworks.name: FTC Act Section 5 — Unfair or Deceptive Acts or Practices (website deception)
frameworks.regulator: Federal Trade Commission (FTC); state attorneys general concurrently under state UDAP
frameworks.citation: Federal Trade Commission Act, Section 5, 15 U.S.C. §45(a); enforcement/penalty authority §5(l), §5(m); .com Disclosures guidance (2013)

penalty.basis: no per se fine for a first §5(a) violation; civil penalties up to $53,088 per violation (2025 adjustment) attach to conduct that violates an FTC rule or a prior order, plus redress/disgorgement; typical band reflects negotiated monetary judgments

obligations: Do not publish false, misleading or deceptive representations about a product or service (the breach is a deceptive claim being present on the site)
Hold a reasonable basis (competent and reliable evidence) for every objective claim before it is published
Material terms and disclosures are clear and conspicuous, not buried in fine print, hyperlinks, or hover text (.com Disclosures)
No dark patterns that trick or trap the consumer (obstructed cancellation, pre-checked add-ons, false urgency, hidden fees)
frameworks.why: Section 5 is the backstop the FTC reaches for when no specific rule fits; almost every misleading headline, fake 'was/now' price, unsupported 'clinically proven' or 'guaranteed results' line on a US site is a §5 exposure.
frameworks.focus: What is the net impression to a reasonable consumer, and what evidence did you hold before you published the claim?

enforcement.summary: First FTC action over suppression of negative reviews; presenting a curated 4-5 star wall as all reviews was a deceptive §5 practice.

frameworks.name: FTC Green Guides — environmental marketing claims (16 CFR Part 260)
frameworks.citation: FTC Act §5; Guides for the Use of Environmental Marketing Claims, 16 CFR Part 260 (Green Guides); §5, 15 U.S.C. §45

penalty.basis: the Guides are interpretive; deceptive green claims are enforced as §5 violations, and where tied to a rule or order carry civil penalties up to $53,088 per violation plus corrective advertising

obligations: Every environmental claim is truthful, substantiated, specific, and qualified so it is not deceptive
frameworks.why: Greenwashing is a stated FTC priority and the Green Guides are the yardstick; vague 'sustainable' or 'carbon-neutral' badges without qualification are the classic finding.
frameworks.focus: What specific, substantiated environmental benefit are you claiming, and can a consumer see the qualification and evidence next to the claim?

frameworks.name: FTC Health Breach Notification Rule (2024 Final Rule)
frameworks.citation: Federal Trade Commission Act; American Recovery and Reinvestment Act 2009 s.13407; 16 CFR Part 318, 16 CFR Part 318 (as amended, final rule published 30 May 2024, effective 29 July 2024)

penalty.basis: Civil penalty up to 53,088 dollars per violation per day (inflation-adjusted) for Rule violations; individual consumer-level counts drive very large totals

obligations: Do not disclose consumers' identifiable health data to advertising or analytics vendors without affirmative express consent
Maintain a breach-notification capability and disclosure
frameworks.why: Non-HIPAA health apps and direct-to-consumer wellness sites wrongly assume they are unregulated; the HBNR reaches exactly the tracker-and-SDK sharing that is visible in their network traffic.
frameworks.focus: Does the app or site share any identifiable health data with third-party advertisers or analytics vendors, and did the consumer affirmatively consent?

enforcement.summary: FTC's first Health Breach Notification Rule action: 1.5m civil penalty for disclosing health data to Facebook, Google, Criteo, Branch and Twilio through tracking pixels and SDKs, and a ban on sharing health data for advertising.

frameworks.name: FTC Made in USA Labeling Rule — origin claims (16 CFR Part 323)
frameworks.citation: FTC Made in USA Labeling Rule; FTC Act §5, 16 CFR Part 323 (effective 13 Aug 2021); §5, 15 U.S.C. §45

penalty.basis: the Labeling Rule is a Trade Regulation Rule; violations carry civil penalties up to $53,088 per violation (2025 adjustment) plus redress

obligations: Do not make an unqualified US-origin claim unless the product is 'all or virtually all' made in the United States
frameworks.why: Since 2021 the FTC has a dedicated rule with per-violation civil penalties for false US-origin claims; 'Made in USA' badges are a specific, checkable claim with real teeth.
frameworks.focus: Is this product 'all or virtually all' made in the US, and if not, is the origin claim properly qualified?

frameworks.name: FTC Endorsement Guides 2023 + Consumer Reviews and Testimonials Rule (16 CFR Part 465)
frameworks.citation: FTC Act §5; Guides Concerning the Use of Endorsements and Testimonials (16 CFR Part 255, revised 2023); Trade Regulation Rule on the Use of Consumer Reviews and Testimonials (16 CFR Part 465, 2024), 16 CFR Part 255 (effective 26 Jun 2023, 88 FR 48092); 16 CFR Part 465 (effective 21 Oct 2024)

penalty.basis: Part 465 is a Trade Regulation Rule, so knowing violations carry civil penalties up to $53,088 per violation (2025 adjustment) plus consumer redress; the Guides themselves are interpretive but breaches are actionable as §5 deception

obligations: Clearly and conspicuously disclose every material connection between an endorser and the brand, near the claim
Do not publish, buy, sell or incentivise fake, AI-generated, or misrepresented reviews (Part 465 binding prohibitions)
Do not misrepresent testimonial results; disclose when depicted results are not typical
frameworks.why: Since 21 Oct 2024 fake and suppressed reviews are not just deception, they carry per-violation civil penalties under a binding rule; undisclosed influencer and affiliate relationships remain the most-cited endorsement failure.
frameworks.focus: Are all reviews genuine and unfiltered, and is every paid or gifted relationship disclosed where the consumer sees the claim?

enforcement.case: FTC v. Fashion Nova, LLC (review suppression)
enforcement.summary: Blocking sub-four-star reviews and displaying only high ratings misrepresented the body of reviews; foundational case now codified into Part 465.

frameworks.name: HIPAA Privacy Rule - Marketing Authorization and Notice of Privacy Practices
frameworks.regulator: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Office for Civil Rights (OCR)
frameworks.citation: Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act; 45 CFR Part 164, 45 CFR 164.508 (marketing authorization); 164.520 (Notice of Privacy Practices); 164.501 (marketing definition)

penalty.basis: Tiered civil monetary penalties per violation, with an annual cap per identical provision (inflation-adjusted; the highest-tier per-violation maximum and the calendar-year cap are both 2,190,294 dollars for 2026); OCR resolution agreements common

obligations: Post a compliant Notice of Privacy Practices and link it from the site
Obtain valid HIPAA authorization before any use or disclosure of PHI for marketing
frameworks.why: A missing Notice of Privacy Practices or PHI used to build marketing lists is the most basic HIPAA failing OCR checks first, and it is visible on the public site.
frameworks.focus: Is a current Notice of Privacy Practices posted and linked, and can the entity show a signed authorization for any PHI used in marketing?

enforcement.case: Gums Dental Care (OCR civil monetary penalty)
enforcement.summary: OCR imposed a 70,000 civil monetary penalty on a solo dental practice over a delayed patient records request, a signal that small practices are within enforcement reach.

frameworks.name: HIPAA Online Tracking Technologies Guidance (OCR Bulletin) and Post-Vacatur Status
frameworks.regulator: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Office for Civil Rights (OCR)
frameworks.citation: HIPAA Privacy and Security Rules; 45 CFR Part 164; OCR guidance 'Use of Online Tracking Technologies by HIPAA Covered Entities and Business Associates', 45 CFR 164.502 (disclosures); 164.308/164.312 (safeguards); OCR bulletin Dec 2022, revised Mar 2024

penalty.basis: HIPAA civil monetary penalties where an impermissible disclosure occurs; separate class-action and FTC exposure runs far higher (see enforcement)

obligations: Prevent impermissible disclosure of PHI to tracking vendors on authenticated and PHI-bearing pages
frameworks.why: A tracking pixel on an appointment or portal page is the single highest-cost web-compliance failure in US healthcare, with aggregate settlement exposure across the hospital pixel-tracking litigation wave above 100m dollars, and it is detectable from network requests.
frameworks.focus: Which third-party trackers load on authenticated and appointment pages, and is each covered by a BAA or removed?

frameworks.name: Professional Advertising Rules - New York (Regents professions incl. dental, nursing, pharmacy; physicians via Educ. Law 6530)
frameworks.regulator: New York State Board for Professional Medical Conduct / Office of the Professions
frameworks.citation: New York Education Law; Rules of the Board of Regents, N.Y. Educ. Law 6530(27); 8 NYCRR 29.1(b)(12) (advertising or soliciting not in the public interest, including false, deceptive or misleading advertising)

penalty.basis: New York State Board for Professional Medical Conduct disciplinary action for professional misconduct (false, deceptive or misleading advertising under N.Y. Educ. Law 6530(27) / 8 NYCRR 29.1(b)(12)). Penalties under N.Y. Public Health Law 230-a: censure and reprimand, licence suspension, limitation, revocation or annulment, and a fine not exceeding USD 10,000 upon each specification of charges of which the licensee is found guilty; no fixed website-specific tariff. Verified on N.Y. Public Health Law 230-a (official) 2026-07-17.

obligations: Keep all advertising truthful, non-misleading, and properly substantiated
frameworks.why: State boards, alongside the FTC, act on misleading treatment claims and inaccurate board-certification statements; the risky language sits on the homepage.
frameworks.focus: Are the board-certification statements accurate and are outcome or superiority claims substantiated?

frameworks.name: Restore Online Shoppers' Confidence Act (ROSCA) — online subscriptions and auto-renewal
frameworks.regulator: Federal Trade Commission (FTC); state AGs under state Automatic Renewal Laws
frameworks.citation: Restore Online Shoppers' Confidence Act; FTC Negative Option Rule (pre-2024 prenotification version, 16 CFR Part 425), 15 U.S.C. §§8401-8405 (esp. §8403); Negative Option Rule 16 CFR Part 425

penalty.basis: ROSCA violations are treated as violations of an FTC rule, so civil penalties up to $53,088 per violation (2025 adjustment) plus redress apply; state Automatic Renewal Laws add parallel penalties

obligations: Clearly disclose all material terms before obtaining billing information
Obtain express informed consent to the negative-option feature before charging
Provide a simple mechanism to cancel and stop future charges
frameworks.why: Subscriptions are a top FTC and state-AG enforcement priority; the exposure sits in unclear renewal disclosure, pre-checked auto-renewal, and cancellation friction.
frameworks.focus: Before you took the card, did you clearly disclose the recurring charge, get separate consent to it, and is cancellation as easy as signup?

frameworks.name: ACA Section 1557 - Notice of Nondiscrimination and Notice of Availability of Language Assistance (45 CFR Part 92)
frameworks.citation: Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act s.1557; HHS 2024 final rule, 45 CFR Part 92, 45 CFR 92.10 (notice of nondiscrimination: provided annually and posted in a conspicuous location on the website, with OCR complaint information and, where required, the Section 1557 Coordinator's contact details); 45 CFR 92.11 (notice of availability of free language assistance services and auxiliary aids, in English and at least the 15 most common non-English languages of the State, posted conspicuously including on the website)

penalty.basis: Enforced by the HHS Office for Civil Rights through the civil-rights framework: corrective-action plans, resolution agreements and, ultimately, suspension or termination of federal financial assistance; private civil-rights liability can follow

obligations: Post the Section 1557 notice of nondiscrimination conspicuously on the website
Post the notice of availability of free language assistance services and auxiliary aids
frameworks.why: The 2024 final rule re-established the notice duties as concrete, website-checkable items - a missing nondiscrimination notice or missing 15-language taglines is visible on the homepage footer in seconds, and it is distinct from the s.504 accessibility duty already screened.
frameworks.focus: Where on your website is your notice of nondiscrimination, and does your language-assistance notice cover the top-15 languages for your State?

frameworks.name: State UDAP / 'mini-FTC' acts — unfair and deceptive practices (advisory overlay)
frameworks.regulator: State Attorneys General; frequently a private right of action for consumers
frameworks.citation: State unfair and deceptive acts and practices (UDAP) statutes; every state has one (e.g., California UCL/FAL, Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §§17200 & 17500; Florida FDUTPA; Massachusetts Ch. 93A; New York GBL §349), Representative anchor: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §17200 (unfair competition) and §17500 (false advertising)

penalty.basis: per-violation penalties vary widely by state (commonly $2,000-$10,000 per violation); many acts add a private right of action, attorneys' fees, and in some states treble or statutory damages

obligations: The same truthful, substantiated, non-deceptive standard as FTC §5 applies at state level, often with a private right of action and, in some states, statutory or treble damages
frameworks.why: Even where the FTC does not act, a deceptive US page is exposed under all fifty states' UDAP laws, several of which let consumers sue directly and recover multiplied damages.
frameworks.focus: Is the claim truthful and substantiated to the same standard a state AG or a consumer plaintiff would apply?

frameworks.name: Telephone Consumer Protection Act — web consent capture for calls and texts
frameworks.regulator: Federal Communications Commission (FCC); private right of action and state AGs
frameworks.citation: Telephone Consumer Protection Act, 47 U.S.C. §227; FCC rules 47 CFR §64.1200; revocation-of-consent rule effective 11 Apr 2025

penalty.basis: private right of action: $500 per negligent violation, up to $1,500 per willful violation, per call or text; class exposure runs to seven and eight figures

obligations: Obtain prior express written consent for autodialed/prerecorded marketing calls and texts at the point of capture
Provide and honour a simple revocation ('STOP' in any reasonable manner), honoured within 10 business days
frameworks.why: TCPA is plaintiff-lawyer territory: each text is its own statutory-damages unit, so a lead form that captures a phone number without proper consent is a class-action magnet.
frameworks.focus: Where is the express-written-consent language, is it unchecked, and does it say consent is not required to buy?
